accroche: In 1960, a Chaucer specialist demonstrates that American Sign Language is a real language, and is attacked by his own colleagues.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1955, Gallaudet University, the only institution of higher education in the world entirely dedicated to deaf students, hires William Stokoe as a professor and head of the English department. His specialty: medieval literature, in particular Chaucer. He then has almost no experience of the deaf world, and discovers upon arriving that what he is being taught as “sign language,” a word-for-word signed English, is not what deaf students actually use among themselves.

## The Structural Proof

Stokoe begins observing and recording this informal language, and in 1960 publishes *Sign Language Structure*, a monograph that would become the founding text of the linguistics of sign languages. In it he shows that each sign of American Sign Language (ASL) breaks down into three simultaneous elements, meaningless in themselves but combinable according to precise rules: the handshape, the location where the sign is produced, the movement that performs it. This is exactly the property that defines a real language rather than a mere code of gestures: the combination of units with no meaning of their own to produce units that have one, as the phonemes of a spoken language combine into words. ASL is therefore neither pantomime nor English translated gesture by gesture: it is a full-fledged language, with its own grammar.

## The Rejection

The demonstration does not convince immediately, least of all at Gallaudet itself. Many colleagues, mostly deaf, regarded ASL at the time as a degraded form of English, a stopgap to be moved beyond rather than studied for its own sake. Legitimizing ASL as a distinct language seemed to threaten efforts to integrate deaf students into a world that speaks and writes English. Stokoe would later recount: “With the exception of one or two colleagues, the entire Gallaudet faculty rudely attacked me, linguistics and the study of signing as a language.” He persists nonetheless, and in 1965 publishes, with Dorothy Casterline and Carl Croneberg, the first dictionary of ASL organized by linguistic principles rather than by the alphabetical order of its English translation.

## What It Shifts

The recognition of ASL as a full-fledged language takes decades to take hold. But it ends up transforming deaf education and the way deafness itself is thought of: no longer only as a hearing deficit to be corrected, but as possible membership in a linguistic and cultural community of its own. Stokoe's method, applied since to hundreds of sign languages around the world, has shown that this structure was not an oddity peculiar to ASL, but a general property of visual-gestural languages. Proof that a language does not need to be spoken to be a language.

carte.punch: In 1960, a Chaucer specialist proves that sign language is a real language.
carte.idee: William Stokoe, a medievalist hired at Gallaudet without knowing ASL, shows in 1960 that each sign breaks down into handshape, location, and movement, combinable like the phonemes of a spoken language. His deaf colleagues attack him: legitimizing ASL seemed to threaten integration.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The writing system Stokoe invents to transcribe the three parameters of the sign.

quiz.question: What does Stokoe demonstrate in 1960 that establishes that ASL is a real language, and not a mere gestural code?
choix: That the signs of ASL can all be translated word for word into English, sentence by sentence
That deaf children learn ASL at exactly the same speed as hearing children learn English
That each sign breaks down into units with no meaning of their own, handshape, location, movement, combinable like the phonemes of a spoken language
That ASL shares most of its vocabulary with French Sign Language, from which it descends
quiz.explication: It is the breakdown into combinable units with no meaning in isolation, handshape, location, movement, that constitutes the structural proof that a language is a language, exactly as phonemes with no meaning of their own combine into meaningful words. ASL is not a gestural copy of English sentence by sentence, and if it shares a distant origin with French Sign Language, that fact proves nothing about its status as an autonomous language.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What was William Stokoe's specialty before he took an interest in sign language?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Stokoe is hired in 1955 as a professor and head of Gallaudet's English department, his specialty being medieval literature, in particular Chaucer, with no prior experience of the deaf world.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Stokoe publish in 1965, with Dorothy Casterline and Carl Croneberg?
choix: An oral rehabilitation method for deaf children
A collection of poems translated into sign language
The first dictionary of ASL organized by linguistic principles
A comparative grammar of ASL and English
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In 1965, Stokoe publishes with Dorothy Casterline and Carl Croneberg the first dictionary of ASL organized by linguistic principles rather than by the alphabetical order of its English translation.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why do some of Stokoe's colleagues, mostly deaf, reject his demonstration?
choix: They thought that legitimizing ASL as a distinct language would threaten integration into an English-speaking world
They judged his notation method too complex to teach
They felt Stokoe lacked the academic authority in linguistics
They feared that recognition of ASL would reduce Gallaudet's funding
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Many colleagues regarded ASL as a degraded form of English to be moved beyond, and legitimizing ASL as a distinct language seemed to threaten efforts to integrate deaf students.
